newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hardline Chechen guerrilla seeks statesman image.
newsitem.headline: Hardline Chechen guerrilla seeks statesman image.

text.p: Chechen presidential candidate Shamil Basayev made his name on the international stage when he seized more than 1,000 hostages in a bloody guerrilla raid on a small south Russian town.

Basayev, fired to action by a string of Russian victories over rebels in the summer of 1995, held a hospital in Budennovsk for almost a week. He beat off Russian commandos and slipped away leaving some 100 dead and the Kremlin in disarray.
The action changed the complexion of the Chechen war. It forced Moscow to talks, brought a previously distant conflict to the Russian interior and gave rebel forces time to regroup.

The raid was also typical of Basayev's personal style since then Chechen leader Dzhokhar Dudayev declared independence from Moscow in 1991, moving Moscow to declare a state of emergency in the region. Basayev decided immediately on a personal protest.
"Shamil made the only proper decision -- he hijacked a plane," says his colour political brochure.
Basayev and comrades forced the pilot to fly to Turkey in order to draw attention to Moscow's policy in Chechnya.
His methods have been controversial but, over 21 months of Russian attempts to break the rebels, proved effective.
Now Basayev seeks the role of statesman, leading Chechnya to the international recognition still withheld by a world community reluctant to anger Russia or appear to endorse past guerrilla tactics.
Basayev is one of four top contenders in Monday's presidential elections.
His proven toughness and promise to ruthlessly stamp out post-war crime has won backers, especially among young people. He has advocated public executions for serious offences.
Basayev has aimed to soften his image, shedding the camouflage fatigues that were almost a second skin for over two years and donning a charcoal greatcoat and paisley neckscarf.
"People should think less about Budennovsk and more about the tens of thousands of innocent people slaughtered in Russian air and artillery attacks during the war," he said recently.
Yet fears among some voters as to how such a controversial figure would portray Chechnya to the outside world and effect relations with Moscow continue.
"I think if Basayev becomes president then Russia will not allow our land to flourish," said 23-year-old librarian Toma after watching one of his campaign appearances.

He has played this down, calling good relations with Moscow "my top priority" and saying that under him "there will never be another war in Chechnya". But he warns that if Russia does attempt another taming of Chechnya, "we will destroy it".
Basayev, who has just turned 32, has run one of the more active presidential campaigns, opening a personal television channel and making frequent stump speeches.
Some detractors say he is smashing wartime rebel unity by attacking political opponents like former chief commander Aslan Maskhadov, calling him a "criminal" and "crook".
In election posters he looks like a man just returned from an African safari, bearded face smiling broadly under a round khaki cap. "Voting for Shamil, you vote for freedom," reads the caption.
Basayev's campaign literature draws comparisons between him and Imam Shamil, a 19th century Caucasian warrior who battled invading Tsarist armies for three decades.
